# Ulnar nerve entrapment

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Upper extremity > Ulnar nerve entrapment*

[Original Article Link](/library/AR0Rpf)

---

## Summary

<u>Ulnar nerve</u> entrapment occurs when the <u>ulnar nerve</u> is compressed, typically at the <u>elbow</u> or the wrist. Compression at the <u>elbow</u> is called <u>cubital tunnel syndrome</u>; compression at the wrist it is referred to as <u>Guyon's canal syndrome</u> or <u>ulnar tunnel syndrome</u>. The compression causes <u>paresthesias</u>, numbness, and/or <u>pain</u> in the <u>ulnar nerve</u> distribution. Depending on the site of compression, the patient may experience <u>weakness</u> in certain hand muscles. Ulnar <u>entrapment neuropathy</u> may be suspected based on clinical symptoms and signs, but it must be confirmed by <u>electromyography</u> (<u>EMG</u>). <u>Conservative treatment</u> involves <u>NSAIDs</u>, behavior modification, and bracing. Severe, persistent, or worsening symptoms require surgical decompression.

---

## Overview of ulnar nerve entrapment

### Course of the <u>ulnar nerve</u>




* The <u>ulnar nerve</u> arises from the <u>medial</u> cord of the <u>brachial plexus</u>, which, in turn, arises from the <u>nerve roots</u> C8–T1.

* From the <u>brachial plexus</u>, the <u>ulnar nerve</u> courses through the <u>medial</u> bicipital sulcus and descends down the <u>medial</u> aspect of the arm <u>medial</u> to the <u>brachial artery</u> to the <u>elbow</u>.

* Passes the <u>medial</u> <u>epicondylar groove</u> at the <u>elbow</u>

* Enters the palm through the <u>Guyon canal</u>

* For more detailed information on motor and sensory innervation, see "<u>Neurovasculature of the upper limbs</u>."





![Cross-section of wrist showing the carpal tunnel and Guyon canal](media/ymd9maq216r2flr4aaa063mr.jpg)

Cross-section of wrist showing the carpal tunnel and Guyon canal




### Ulnar neuropathy at the <u>elbow</u> and wrist [[1]](/library/iPWJel0)[[2]](/library/phWLUO0)




The <u>ulnar nerve</u> is most commonly compressed at or near the cubital tunnel of the <u>elbow</u> and <u>Guyon canal</u> of the wrist.




|  | Cubital tunnel syndrome | Guyon canal syndrome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Location | <br>* At the <u>medial epicondyle</u> of the <u>humerus</u> (cubital tunnel)<br><br> | <br>* At the wrist (within the <u>Guyon canal</u>)<br><br> |
| Etiology | <br><br>* Prolonged <u>flexion</u> of or other <u>stress</u> on the <u>elbow</u><br><br>* Leaning at the desk<br><br>* Compression during <u>general anesthesia</u><br><br>* <u>Sports injuries</u> (e.g., baseball, bodybuilding)<br><br>* <u>Blunt trauma</u> at the <u>elbow</u><br><br>* Masses at the cubital tunnel (e.g., <u>hematomas</u>)<br><br>* Metabolic conditions associated with neuropathy (e.g., <u>diabetes</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Sports injuries</u> e.g.,<br><br>* Cycling (likely caused by direct pressure from the handlebars)<br><br>* Racket sport<br><br>* See also, ''<u>Compression neuropathies in sport</u>.''<br><br>* <u>Blunt trauma</u> at the wrist (e.g., hook of <u>hamate</u> <u>fracture</u> causing <u>Guyon canal</u> compression)<br><br>* Masses at the <u>Guyon canal</u> (e.g., <u>ganglion cysts</u>)<br><br>* Fibrous bands<br><br>* Anomalous muscle insertions<br><br>* <u>Ulnar artery</u> <u>aneurysm</u> or <u>thrombosis</u><br><br><br> |
| Motor deficit | <br>* Muscle <u>atrophy</u> and <u>weakness</u> (less common than sensory symptoms)<br><br>* Loss of dexterity<br><br>* Decreased grip strength<br><br>* Difficulty lifting<br><br> | <br>* <u>Weakness</u> and <u>atrophy</u> of the intrinsic hand muscles innervated by the <u>ulnar nerve</u><br><br> |
| Sensory deficit | <br><br>* <u>Paresthesia</u> or sensory loss of the <u>palmar</u> and <u>dorsal</u> aspects of the <u>medial</u> side of the hand, little finger, and ulnar side of the ring finger<br><br>* <u>Referred pain</u> in the forearm<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Paresthesia</u> or sensory loss of the <u>palmar</u> and <u>dorsal</u> aspects of the <u>medial</u> side of the hand, little finger, and ulnar side of the ring finger<br><br> |

---

## Clinical features

### Motor symptoms




* Entrapment at the <u>elbow</u>

* Less common than sensory complaints and range from mild to severe <u>weakness</u>

* Muscle <u>atrophy</u> and <u>weakness</u>

* Loss of dexterity

* Decreased grip strength

* Difficulty lifting

* Entrapment at the wrist: <u>weakness</u> and <u>atrophy</u> of the intrinsic hand muscles innervated by the <u>ulnar nerve</u>





### Sensory symptoms




* Entrapment at the <u>elbow</u>

* <u>Paresthesia</u> or sensory loss of <u>palmar</u> and <u>dorsal</u> aspects of the <u>medial</u> side of the hand, little finger, and ulnar side of the ring finger

* <u>Referred pain</u> in the forearm

* Entrapment at the wrist

* Variable <u>paresthesia</u> or sensory loss of the <u>palmar</u> and <u>dorsal</u> aspects of the <u>medial</u> side of the hand, little finger, and ulnar side of the ring finger

* Compression of the <u>ulnar nerve</u> at the wrist is divided into three zones and exam findings often correlate with the site of injury.

* Zone I: lesions <u>proximal</u> to the bifurcation of the <u>ulnar nerve</u> 

* Motor and sensory symptoms (i.e., sensory loss in the <u>palmar</u> surface of the little finger and <u>medial</u> aspect of the ring finger) possible

* Sensory features similar to those caused by <u>proximal</u> lesions at the <u>elbow</u>

* Zone II: lesions at the deep motor branch cause motor symptoms only

* Zone III: lesions at the <u>distal</u> sensory branch cause sensory symptoms only





### <u>Physical examination</u>




* Ulnar claw 

* Palsy of the 3<sup>rd</sup> and 4<sup>th</sup> <u>lumbricals</u> with preserved function of the extrinsic flexors

* Present at rest, increases when the patient is asked to extend the fingers

* Mainly seen in <u>distal</u> <u>ulnar nerve</u> injuries

* Froment sign 

* <u>Flexion</u> of the thumb at the <u>interphalangeal joint</u> elicited when tightly pressing together the tips of the index finger and thumb, or when tightly <u>adducting</u> the thumb against the 2nd <u>metacarpal</u> (e.g., pinching a piece of paper using the thumb)

* Due to <u>weakness</u> of the <u>adductor pollicis muscle</u> and the unopposed action of <u>flexor pollicis longus</u>

* Wartenberg sign

* Persistent <u>abduction</u> of the little finger

* Due to <u>weakness</u> of the third <u>palmar</u> <u>interosseous muscle</u>

* Jeanne sign

* Hyperextension of the <u>MCP joint</u> of the thumb with key pinch movement

* Due to loss of function of the <u>adductor pollicis muscle</u> and predominance of the <u>extensor pollicis longus</u> and the <u>abductor pollicis brevis</u>

* <u>Tinel sign</u>: tapping on the <u>medial epicondyle</u> of the <u>humerus</u> elicits marked <u>paresthesias</u> in the ulnar portion of the hand





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Ulnar claw</u> deformity is mainly seen in <u>distal</u> <u>ulnar nerve</u> injuries, while difficulty making a fist occurs in <u>proximal</u> <u>ulnar nerve</u> injuries.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Proximal</u> and <u>distal</u> lesions of the <u>ulnar nerve</u> lead to <u>claw hand deformity</u>.

## Diagnosis

* <u>Electrodiagnostic studies</u> (<u>nerve conduction studies</u> and <u>EMG</u>): identify the level of nerve compression

* <u>Ultrasound</u> and <u>MRI</u>: confirm <u>EMG</u> findings and identify the cause of compression

---

## Treatment

* <u>Conservative therapy</u> [[2]](/library/phWLUO0)

* Modify behavior (e.g., avoid prolonged resting on <u>elbow</u>, repeated <u>flexion</u> of <u>elbow</u>)

* <u>Analgesia</u> (e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>)

* Bracing at night

* Surgical decompression: if clinical features are severe, persistent (i.e., lasting more than 6 to 12 weeks), or progressively worsen despite <u>conservative therapy</u>
